To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the optical disc of spiral galaxies is a self-similar system and the classical Tully–Freeman and Freeman scaling laws are defined on annular boundaries that do not conform to the self-similarity of the disc.

there are self-similar scaling laws defined on an annular region in the optical disc of galaxies which, corresponding to the conventional Tully-Fisher relation and Freeman law defined on the outer annular boundary, are such that there are similar scaling relations defined on the inner annular boundary.

the hypothesis that galaxy disc dynamics is self-similar leads to the conclusion that the Tully-Fishers and Freeman scaling laws are both valid, and that a new scaling law, which is the ratio of the surface density to the rotation velocity squared, is also valid.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether galaxy discs are governed by a universal law of dynamics.
the question of how to define the Tully-Fishing rotation velocity, Vmax, and the galaxy radius Rmax, for the Freeman law, for a sample of galaxies.
the hypothesis that the dynamics of galaxy discs conform to a self-similar scaling law.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Tully-Fishers and Freeman scaling laws, when applied to the optical discs of galaxies, are both manifestations of the same underlying self-similar scaling law.
, in the context of the self-similar hypothesis, the data provide evidence for a refined Tully–Fisher relationship which is insensitive to the definition of Vmax.
the Tully-Fisherscaling laws are a direct consequence of the self-similar dynamics of galaxy discs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in addition to providing a new scaling law which is defined on the inner disc, the analysis provides a means by which to objectively define Vmax and Rmax and provides a means by to refine the Tully-Fischer relationship.

the hypothesis of self-similar dynamics in discs leads to a new scaling law, the Tully-Fisherman scaling law, which is a generalisation of the Tully-Fishe law, and which, as we show, is the most natural way to define the Tully-Fischer scaling law.
we have identified an annular region in the optical disc which, when used in the construction of the Tully-Fischer and Freeman scaling laws, leads to an objective, robust and self-consistent result.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Tully-Fisherscaling law is a consequence of the self-similarity of galaxy discs and is not a fundamental property of galaxies.
the Tully-Fisherscaling law, and the Freeman scaling law, are not two separate scaling laws but rather two sides of the same scaling law.
, for the first time, we are led by the data to a new and refined Tully-Fisherscaling law.
